title: Localization transitions of diffusion dynamics in physical networks
authors: Jun Yamamoto, Ivan Bonamassa, Márton Pósfai
abstract: Network diffusion underlies many transport phenomena, with Laplacian modes setting how information spreads and relaxes. In physical networks, however, connectivity alone is not enough: node volumes introduce local dwell times that regulate how flow is stored before being propagated. Here we show that physical heterogeneity reshapes topology-driven localization, with the degree-volume ratio emerging as the relevant disorder parameter. We solve an analytical model in which ratio detuning qualitatively reorganizes the Laplacian spectrum, and demonstrate in empirical networks how degree-volume correlations shift extremal eigenmodes away from the nodes selected by topology alone. Our results reveal a general feature-rich-driven mechanism for localization control, showing that physicality non-trivially reshapes the disorder landscape governing network dynamics.
summary: This paper analyzes how physical node volumes modify information flow dynamics (diffusion) on complex networks. It demonstrates that connectivity alone is insufficient, showing that the degree-volume ratio acts as the critical disorder parameter governing spectral localization. This provides a general framework for understanding how local physical constraints reshape global network transport properties.
main_problem: The study investigates how physical heterogeneity, introduced via node volumes, alters the localization patterns of diffusion dynamics in complex networks beyond what is predicted by topology alone.
main_result: The relevant disorder parameter controlling spectral localization shifts from simple degree correlations to the degree-volume ratio ($d/v$), revealing a feature-rich mechanism for controlling network transport properties.
method: The authors employ spectral analysis of the node-weighted Laplacian, using the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) to quantify mode localization in both solvable defect models and empirical networks.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a connected simple network $G$ with nodes possessing degrees ($k_i$) and associated volumes ($v_i$). The dynamics are governed by the node-weighted Laplacian operator, $L_P$.
key_observables: Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) of extremal eigenvectors ($\psi_2, \psi_N$), and the Jaccard index comparing localization sets defined by degree, volume, or ratio.
important_parameters: The primary control parameter is the degree-volume ratio ($r = d/v$) or the correlation exponent $\alpha$ governing how volumes scale with degrees ($	ext{e.g.} v_i \propto k_i^\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving an analytical defect model and comparing results across synthetic random graphs (ER, CL) and real-world physical networks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spectral shifts in the defect model based on $d/v$, showing localization thresholds; other figures compare IPR vs. correlation exponent $\alpha$ for different graph types, confirming the shift to ratio control.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and the limitations of topology-only analysis, through developing a solvable defect model using spectral theory, and finally validating these findings by analyzing empirical networks across varying degree-volume correlations ($\alpha$).
why_interesting: While focused on classical diffusion, the concept of localization control via an emergent ratio parameter ($k/v$) is analogous to how interaction strengths or geometric constraints can dictate quantum state confinement in engineered quantum systems.
